reviewBoundary: Three complete original senior paired-reading practices, each one three-question information text plus one four-question narrative/expository/argument text. Same-author all-option and evidence review only; no independent learner calibration.

units.title: Backstage helpers and a letter that travelled
units.alignmentNote: Two complete original passages, three and four four-choice questions, following National I final structure. Old source supplies a level/family reference only.

materials.title: A first look behind the stage
materials.text:
The Lantern Youth Theatre is offering a backstage introduction on Sunday, 18 June. Young people aged fifteen to eighteen can try simple lighting cues, organise props and learn how a stage team communicates during a performance. No previous theatre experience is needed.

The morning session runs from 09:30 to 12:00, and the afternoon session from 13:30 to 16:00. Choose one when applying; both cover the same activities. Each group has twelve places. A place is confirmed only after the theatre sends an acceptance email. Sending the form alone does not reserve a place.

Wear closed shoes and clothes that allow comfortable movement. The workshop includes walking between stage and control areas, with some stairs. Contact the team before booking if you need information about access. Do not assume every part of the route can be reached without steps.

The fee is eight pounds, including all workshop materials. Participants should bring their own water. There is no public show at the end, and family members cannot remain in the working areas. A waiting space is available in the foyer.

Please arrive fifteen minutes before your session. Under-eighteens need a parent or guardian consent form; eighteen-year-olds sign their own. If you cannot attend, notify the theatre by Friday so another applicant can be offered the place. The session is an introduction to backstage work, not a qualification to operate theatre equipment independently.

questions.prompt: Which applicant fits the stated entry conditions?
options: A thirteen-year-old professional actor
A sixteen-year-old with no theatre experience
A parent who wants to stay on the stage throughout
An adult applying without choosing a session
questions.explanation: Age15–18 and no experience requirement allow sixteen-year-old beginner. Other choices fail age/application/access rules.

questions.prompt: When should an afternoon participant arrive?
questions.explanation: Afternoon begins13:30; arrival15min earlier is13:15. Others are start/previous end/final end.

questions.prompt: What should a participant understand about the session?
options: Every route is guaranteed to have no steps
It ends with a public performance
It does not authorise independent equipment operation
Application automatically confirms a place
questions.explanation: Final sentence limits qualification. Public show/automatic place/step-free guarantee are expressly denied.

materials.title: The letter behind the drawer
materials.text:
While helping my grandfather move a desk, I found an envelope behind a drawer. It carried a stamp and an address, but no mark to show that it had travelled through the post. My grandfather recognised his own handwriting before he opened it.

The letter was to a friend he had met at college. They had planned to keep in touch, but work and moving house had made their messages less frequent. He had written this one after finding an old photograph, then put it aside while looking for the correct address. Somehow, it had slipped behind the drawer.

I asked whether we should send it now. He read it again and laughed at a sentence promising to write more often. The promise was more than thirty years old. He did not want to post the page as if no time had passed. Instead, he wrote a new letter explaining the discovery and enclosed a copy of the old one.

Finding the friend took longer. The address on the envelope no longer belonged to him. My grandfather contacted the college's former-student office, which offered to pass on a message without giving us anyone's private details. A reply arrived several weeks later.

The friend remembered the photograph and sent a picture of his own family. He also admitted that he had once begun a reply that remained unfinished in a notebook. Both men had imagined the silence belonged entirely to the other.

They now exchange occasional letters. My grandfather keeps the original behind glass on his desk, with the date of its discovery written below. It is no longer waiting to be sent. It records a message that missed its moment, then helped create another. I had thought finding the address would be the main problem. In the end, the more interesting task was finding a way to acknowledge the years between the two pages.

questions.prompt: Why was the old letter not sent originally?
options: The desk was designed as a post box
It was set aside while the address was being checked
The college had banned correspondence
The friend had refused every letter
questions.explanation: Grandfather paused to find correct address and letter slipped behind drawer. Refusal/ban/post-box design not stated.

questions.prompt: Why does the grandfather write a new letter?
options: To explain the discovery and recognise the elapsed time
To demand the old stamp be refunded
To remove all mention of college
To pretend the old promise was made yesterday
questions.explanation: New letter acknowledges decades and encloses copy. Pretence/removing college/refund are not purpose.

questions.prompt: How does the college office help?
options: It writes a fictional reply
It guarantees an immediate answer
It publishes the friend’s address for everyone
It passes on a message while protecting private details
questions.explanation: Office offers message forwarding without disclosure. Public address/fiction/immediate guarantee contradict account.

questions.prompt: What do the two men discover about their silence?
options: Only one had ever wanted to write
Each had left part of the communication unfinished
Both had destroyed every photograph
Neither recognised the other’s name
questions.explanation: Old unsent letter and friend’s unfinished reply show shared interruption. Other choices contradict remembered photo and reply.

units.title: A park survey and the shade above a street
units.alignmentNote: Two complete original passages, three and four four-choice questions, following National I final structure. Old source supplies a level/family reference only.

materials.title: Help map the park’s quiet places
materials.text:
Merefield Park is recruiting volunteers for a one-day sound survey on Saturday, 9 September. The project will record how sound varies across the park during ordinary public use. Volunteers will note what they hear and take short readings with equipment supplied by the organisers.

Choose a morning shift from 08:00 to 11:00 or an afternoon shift from 14:00 to 17:00. Training takes place at the start of each shift, so late arrivals may be unable to participate. No specialist experience is required, but volunteers must be at least sixteen and able to follow a fixed observation procedure.

Work is done in pairs at assigned locations. Volunteers should not choose only places they already consider quiet. Each pair will record the time, location and nearby activities as well as the reading. The survey concerns sound levels and sources, not the content of private conversations; identifiable speech should not be recorded.

Wear suitable shoes for paths that may be uneven and bring water. The equipment is provided, but transport to the meeting point is each volunteer's responsibility. There is no participation fee. A short summary of findings will be sent to volunteers later in the autumn.

Apply by 1 September, stating your preferred shift. Confirmation will name the meeting point and explain any changes due to weather. The survey is an initial snapshot, not proof that a particular part of the park is always quiet. Volunteers should report the conditions they observe rather than try to produce the result they expect.

questions.prompt: Why are volunteers assigned locations?
options: To let everyone arrive whenever they wish
To ensure no one hears any park activity
To collect the words of private conversations
To avoid observing only places already expected to be quiet
questions.explanation: Assignment counters selective quiet-place choice. Silence/late arrival/private speech collection are not goals.

questions.prompt: What must a pair record besides the sound reading?
options: Every nearby person’s name
A guarantee about the whole year
Only their favourite part of the park
Time, location and nearby activities
questions.explanation: Specified contextual metadata supports interpretation. Names/preferences/year guarantee are not required.

questions.prompt: What does the survey claim to provide?
options: Free transport to the park
A professional qualification for every volunteer
An initial picture under observed conditions
Proof that every location is permanently quiet
questions.explanation: Final paragraph explicitly limits snapshot. Permanent proof/qualification/transport are not promised.

materials.title: The shade is part of the street
materials.text:
On a hot day, two nearby streets can feel surprisingly different. One may have broad tree canopies, while the other offers little shelter from direct sunlight. The contrast is a reminder that the temperature reported for a town does not fully describe the conditions a person encounters while walking through it.

Shade changes exposure to sunlight. Trees can also affect their surroundings through the movement of water from leaves into the air. The result depends on many conditions, including the tree, the available water, the street's shape and the weather. It would be misleading to promise that planting any tree will produce the same reduction in heat everywhere.

Design also involves space and time. A young tree does not immediately supply the canopy of a mature one. Roots need suitable conditions, and branches must coexist with buildings, paths and services. Planting is therefore a beginning that requires continued care rather than a complete intervention at the moment of installation.

The experience of a street is not uniform either. Someone waiting at a crossing may remain in one exposed place longer than someone passing through. The location of shade can matter as much as its total area. A shaded patch that misses the place where people must wait may offer less practical relief than its size suggests.

These details complicate simple comparisons, but they also make planning more useful. Observing where people walk, stop and sit can connect environmental measures with everyday use. Residents' accounts can identify uncomfortable locations, while measurements help describe the conditions and evaluate changes.

A cooler street is not created by a symbol of a tree on a plan. It develops through a living structure in a particular place, used by people with different routes and routines. Attention to those relationships can turn a broad aim into decisions about where shade is needed, what can grow there and how it will be maintained.

questions.prompt: What does the contrast between nearby streets illustrate?
options: A town-level temperature does not fully describe personal street conditions
Shade has no relation to sunlight
Every street in a town has exactly the same heat exposure
Walking speed alone determines the weather
questions.explanation: Local exposure differs within town. Uniformity/no shade effect/speed controlling weather contradict argument.

questions.prompt: Why does the writer discuss young trees?
options: They instantly offer a mature canopy
They need no space below ground
Their future shade requires growth and continued care
Their location never matters
questions.explanation: Young-tree section stresses time/root conditions/maintenance. Other claims reverse it.

questions.prompt: What does the crossing example show?
options: Waiting people always move faster
Only total shaded area matters
Every patch offers identical relief
Shade should be placed where people actually spend time
questions.explanation: Exposure at necessary waiting points makes location/use important. Area-only/equal relief overlook it.

questions.prompt: Which planning approach does the passage support?
options: Assuming installation completes the project
Replacing all observations with a tree symbol
Combining environmental conditions with observed use and maintenance needs
Planting identical trees without checking the site
questions.explanation: Whole passage links site/living tree/human routine/care. Other choices deny those dependencies.

units.title: A collection of letters and an unfinished ending
units.alignmentNote: Two complete original passages, three and four four-choice questions, following National I final structure. Old source supplies a level/family reference only.

materials.title: Letters from ordinary journeys
materials.text:
The Northbank Local Archive invites contributions to an exhibition about everyday journeys made between 1960 and 2000. Letters, postcards and short written recollections may be considered. The focus is ordinary travel for work, study, family visits or holidays rather than only exceptional expeditions.

Please send a description and digital image first. Do not post an original without an agreement from the archive. Staff will discuss whether a loan, a copy or a recorded account is most suitable. Offering an item does not guarantee its inclusion, and contributors retain ownership unless a separate donation agreement is made.

For each item, provide dates and places as accurately as possible. Approximate information is welcome when clearly marked as such. Distinguish what the document states from details remembered later. A recollection can add valuable context without being treated as words that were written on the original page.

Before submitting correspondence, consider the privacy of other people mentioned. Archive staff will discuss display permissions and may recommend showing only part of an item. The exhibition is public; private contact details and sensitive passages will not automatically be included merely because they appear in a contributed letter.

Initial proposals should arrive by 30 November. Selected contributors will receive a draft label to check factual details. This check does not provide control over the whole exhibition narrative. The aim is a varied account of everyday mobility, with each contribution identified clearly enough for visitors to understand what kind of source they are reading.

questions.prompt: What should a potential contributor send first?
options: The original without contacting staff
A description and digital image
A signed transfer of every family document
A demand for guaranteed inclusion
questions.explanation: Initial description/image required; original only after agreement. Inclusion/blanket transfer not required.

questions.prompt: How should later memories be presented?
options: As if they were printed on the original page
As context distinguished from the original written record
As proof that every other account is false
Only with all uncertain dates removed
questions.explanation: Recollection adds context while its origin remains clear. Other choices misattribute or overclaim.

questions.prompt: What does checking a draft label allow?
options: Automatic display of private contact details
A guarantee that no other letters will be shown
Control over the entire exhibition narrative
Correction of factual details about the contribution
questions.explanation: Draft-label check is factual, not full editorial control or privacy waiver/exclusivity.

materials.title: Where a story chooses to stop
materials.text:
Readers sometimes describe an ending as unfinished when it does not tell them what happens to every character. Yet the absence of a complete future history does not necessarily mean that a story has failed to end. The more useful question may be what kind of completion the narrative has taught its readers to expect.

A mystery can promise an explanation of an event. If the central puzzle is simply abandoned, dissatisfaction may follow from that unfulfilled promise. A story organised around a relationship may make a different demand. Its decisive moment could be a change in how two people understand one another, even if their later lives remain unknown.

This distinction does not divide all writing neatly into closed and open forms. A single ending can settle one question while leaving another active. The reader may know who sent the letter but remain uncertain whether its recipient will answer. What is resolved and what remains matters more than attaching one general label to the final page.

Writers also influence expectation through emphasis. If an apparently minor object receives unusual attention, readers may begin to expect it to return. That expectation can be fulfilled, redirected or deliberately frustrated. But calling a choice deliberate does not by itself establish that it is effective. The surrounding work must give readers a basis for understanding what the absence contributes.

Discussion becomes more precise when readers identify the question they feel has been left open. One may want an event explained; another may be troubled by a character's unresolved responsibility. They need not agree about the ending to describe their different responses carefully.

An ending is therefore not simply the point where information runs out. It is a decision about where the reader's work changes. Some questions are answered, others are carried beyond the page, and the balance shapes the experience of the whole story. Evaluating that balance requires returning to the promises made along the way.

questions.prompt: What does the first paragraph propose?
options: Count the number of pages after the main event
Require a future biography of every character
Treat all uncertain endings as failures
Judge completion in relation to expectations created by the story
questions.explanation: It asks what completion narrative has led readers to expect. Biographies/universal failure/page counts not criteria.

questions.prompt: Why are a mystery and a relationship story compared?
options: They may promise different kinds of resolution
Relationships never involve events
One always has more characters
Only mysteries can be written well
questions.explanation: Examples distinguish central explanation from relational change. Character count/quality hierarchy/no events unsupported.

questions.prompt: What caution is made about deliberate frustration?
options: Intention alone does not prove the choice works
Writers cannot influence expectation
Every deliberate choice must succeed
Readers should never notice repeated objects
questions.explanation: The text requires surrounding basis beyond claiming deliberateness. Other choices reverse that caution.

questions.prompt: How can readers make disagreement more precise?
options: Ignore the story’s earlier emphasis
Use only the label open ending
Demand agreement before discussion
Name the unresolved question troubling them
questions.explanation: Specific event/responsibility questions clarify responses. General label/forced agreement/ignored emphasis do not.
